clue.text: Sort of case this may initiate?

definitions.text: Sort of case this may initiate?

parts.words: Sort of case this may initiate?
parts.note: read two ways: a barrister's instructions start a legal case, and the word put before 'case' makes a kind of bag for papers

explanation.surface: A riddle asking what might set off some kind of case.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'sort of case' is a document case for carrying papers; the same word is also the instructions that launch a lawsuit.
explanation.definitionFit: A barrister's instructions start a lawsuit, and the word also prefixes 'case' to name a document bag.

clue.text: Sits on horse, also, holding ends of tether

indicators.note: holding means the word for 'also' contains the next piece

parts.note: besides means also, in addition

indicators.note: the ends of a word are its first and last letters

explanation.surface: A rider mounts while keeping hold of the tether.
explanation.walkthrough: 'holding' puts TR, the first and last letters of 'tether', inside BESIDES.
explanation.definitionFit: To bestride a horse is to sit astride it, one leg either side.

clue.text: Land it, getting support from half-hearted partner

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: half-hearted means one of the two middle letters of the partner word is dropped

parts.note: an ally is a partner

explanation.surface: Someone lands it with support from a lukewarm partner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'half-hearted' drops one of the twin Ls at the centre of ALLY, leaving ALY, which supports IT in this down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: A country, a land in Europe.

clue.text: Alfred disturbed Albert a trifle

indicators.note: disturbed means the letters are jumbled out of their order

parts.note: Al is a short form of the name Albert

explanation.surface: Alfred upset Albert just a little.
explanation.walkthrough: 'disturbed' rearranges ALFRED plus AL to make the word.
explanation.definitionFit: Falderal is nonsense or a showy trinket, something of no consequence.

clue.text: Female Scottish economist was relieved

parts.note: a lady is a female
Adam Smith was the Scottish economist who wrote The Wealth of Nations

explanation.surface: A Scottish woman economist felt relief.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is descriptive: Ladysmith, a South African town, was famously relieved in 1900 after a siege in the Boer War.
explanation.definitionFit: The besieged South African town's relief in the Boer War is its best-known historical event.

clue.text: German's air was deceptive

definitions.meaning: a German art song, a setting of a poem

explanation.definitionFit: A Schubert-style song in German, and the past of telling falsehoods.

clue.text: A dying roar from him when ruined

definitions.text: A dying roar from him when ruined

indicators.note: when ruined means the letters of the phrase are wrecked and reassembled

explanation.surface: A ruined man gives out a dying roar.
explanation.walkthrough: 'when ruined' rearranges A DYING ROAR. In Wilde's novel the hero's portrait decays; he dies when he slashes it, with a terrible cry.
explanation.definitionFit: Wilde's character dies with a scream when he finally destroys his corrupted portrait.

clue.text: Action from City against those investing, maybe

definitions.text: Action from City against those investing, maybe

parts.words: Action from City against those investing, maybe
parts.note: looks like a financial lawsuit, but 'investing' is the old military sense of besieging, and the city's action is a sally out at its besiegers

explanation.surface: A London financial firm takes legal action against its investors.
explanation.walkthrough: 'City' suggests London's financial district and 'investing' money; to invest a town is to lay siege to it.
explanation.definitionFit: A sally by troops from a besieged place against the attacking force.

clue.text: Give in, deviously persuaded like this?

indicators.note: deviously means the letters go a crooked way, out of order

parts.note: led, as in led on, means persuaded

explanation.surface: Someone yielded, having been cunningly talked round.
explanation.walkthrough: 'deviously' rearranges GIVE IN to give INVEIG, followed by LED.
explanation.definitionFit: Coaxed someone by flattery or trickery into doing something.

clue.text: One bird or another, seen round river with duck

indicators.note: seen round means the other bird is put around the next letters

parts.note: a hen is another bird
a duck in cricket is a score of zero, O

explanation.surface: A birdwatcher spots one bird or another near a river with a duck.
explanation.walkthrough: 'seen round' puts HEN around R and O.
explanation.definitionFit: A long-legged wading bird of riverbanks.

clue.text: Trifles, unlike 23

definitions.meaning: 23 across is a strong ale, so its opposite is weak ale

explanation.definitionFit: Weak ale in the old sense, and by extension anything of little consequence.

clue.text: Wet movement here to split the right?

parts.note: to rive is to split or tear apart
R is the abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: A question of whether a damp political movement will split the right wing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wet' and 'right' suggest politics (a wet is a moderate Tory); the definition means a place where water moves.
explanation.definitionFit: Water flows along a channel in a stream's bed.

clue.text: Makes sound agreement, as Times does with this

definitions.meaning: words agree in sound at their endings
the newspaper's name ends in the same sound as this word

explanation.definitionFit: Words that chime at their endings agree in sound, as the paper's name does.

clue.text: Start of play in Oval — may emerge from this

definitions.text: Start of play in Oval — may emerge from this

parts.words: Start of play in Oval — may emerge from this
parts.note: the cricketers walk out from their clubhouse at the start of play at a ground

explanation.surface: At the start of a match at the Oval, players come out from somewhere.
explanation.walkthrough: THE OVAL is a London cricket ground; batsmen walk out to the pitch from the clubhouse at the boundary. 'Start of play' tempts a first-letter pick (P), which leads nowhere.
explanation.definitionFit: The cricket ground's clubhouse, where players change and emerge onto the field.

clue.text: Nobody in ancient Rome was such a seaman

definitions.text: Nobody in ancient Rome was such a seaman

parts.words: Nobody in ancient Rome was such a seaman
parts.note: Roman sailors had no underwater craft, so none served below the waves

explanation.surface: A claim about which kind of sailor ancient Rome never had.
explanation.walkthrough: The Romans had galleys but no undersea boats, so no Roman sailor served beneath the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: A sailor serving in an underwater vessel, a modern invention.

clue.text: Doctor with a dull yearning operates in theatre

parts.note: mat (or matt) means dull, without shine
an urge is a yearning

explanation.surface: A doctor with a vague longing performs surgery in the operating theatre.
explanation.walkthrough: 'operates in theatre' suggests a surgeon, but the theatre is the stage; the definition describes the person by what they do.
explanation.definitionFit: A dramatist or literary adviser works in the playhouse.

clue.text: He ain't mixing with company, right?

definitions.text: He ain't mixing with company, right?

indicators.note: mixing means the letters are stirred together into a new order

explanation.surface: A colloquial remark that this fellow doesn't socialise, does he?
explanation.walkthrough: 'mixing' rearranges HEAINT with CO and R. The whole clue also defines: a hermit does not mix with company.
explanation.definitionFit: A religious recluse who withdraws from society.

clue.text: Furious female to put off this male

indicators.note: put off means the given letters are removed from the name

parts.note: Alecto is one of the Furies of Greek myth
taken as written

explanation.surface: An angry woman tries to deter a man.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Furious' means one of the Furies, not angry; 'put off' removes TO from ALECTO.
explanation.definitionFit: A man's first name, short for Alexander.

clue.text: Repeated comment on Alice's growing surprise

definitions.text: Repeated comment on Alice's growing surprise

parts.words: Repeated comment on Alice's growing surprise
parts.note: in Wonderland, Alice grows huge and says the same ungrammatical word twice in astonishment

explanation.surface: Alice keeps saying the same thing as her surprise mounts.
explanation.walkthrough: Alice, literally growing after eating the cake, cries the comparative word twice over: 'growing' is both her size and her surprise.
explanation.definitionFit: Lewis Carroll's Alice exclaims the doubled comparative as she shoots up in height.

clue.text: Displayed by weatherman in his other map

indicators.note: in means the letters run inside the following words

explanation.surface: A forecaster shows something on his other chart.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' points to the letters running through HIS OTHER MAP.
explanation.definitionFit: A line on a weather chart joining places of equal temperature.

clue.text: Comedy hit

definitions.meaning: the low shoe of classical comic actors, standing for comedy as the buskin stands for tragedy

explanation.definitionFit: The classical comic actor's slipper symbolises comedy, and a hard blow is a punch.

clue.text: A leader of mission abroad perhaps, needing to conceal craft

definitions.text: A leader of mission abroad perhaps, needing to conceal craft

indicators.note: the leader of a word is its first letter
to conceal means the craft is hidden inside the jumbled letters
perhaps signals that the word abroad is a loose arrangement of its letters

parts.note: SS, steamship, is a craft

explanation.surface: A diplomat heading a mission overseas must keep his skills under wraps.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' rearranges ABROAD to BAADOR, and 'to conceal' puts SS inside it; A and M (first letter of 'mission') come first.
explanation.definitionFit: A senior diplomat heads a nation's mission in a foreign country.

clue.text: Do blunt bridge players call these themselves?

definitions.text: Do blunt bridge players call these themselves?

parts.words: Do blunt bridge players call these themselves?
parts.note: blunt people are said to name a digging tool exactly as it is, and in bridge that is also a suit

explanation.surface: A question about how plain-speaking card players name a suit.
explanation.walkthrough: Plain speakers 'call a spade a spade'; bridge players naming the black suit would call it just that.
explanation.definitionFit: The highest suit in bridge, and the tools a frank speaker refuses to call by any other name.

clue.text: Duke of Milan wanting us to be successful

indicators.note: wanting means lacking, so the given letters are taken out

parts.note: prosperous means successful
taken as written

explanation.surface: A duke hopes for success for all of us.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wanting' removes US from PROSPEROUS. In Shakespeare's The Tempest, the magician is the rightful Duke of Milan.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's magician in The Tempest is the deposed ruler of that Italian city.

clue.text: Expert, of course, can be replaced, by George!

definitions.text: Expert, of course, can be replaced, by George!

parts.words: Expert, of course, can be replaced, by George!
parts.note: an expert who steers a ship or plane on its course, who can be swapped for the automatic device airmen nicknamed George

explanation.surface: An exclamation that even an expert can of course be replaced.
explanation.walkthrough: 'by George!' looks like an oath; George was RAF slang for the automatic steering device.
explanation.definitionFit: A guide who steers a vessel or aircraft, whose job an autopilot can do.

clue.text: Sound as a bell so swallowed strong drink

indicators.note: swallowed means the word so takes the bell's sound inside it

parts.note: taken as written
ting is the sound a small bell makes

explanation.surface: Someone perfectly healthy downed a strong drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sound as a bell' looks like the idiom for in good health, but it is the ringing noise TING, which 'swallowed' puts inside SO.
explanation.definitionFit: An old name for a strong, well-aged beer.

clue.text: One led by removing heads, with poor result

indicators.note: removing heads means the first letter of each of the three words is dropped

explanation.surface: Someone leading by beheading gets a poor outcome.
explanation.walkthrough: 'removing heads' takes O, L and B from ONE LED BY, leaving NE, ED and Y.
explanation.definitionFit: Lacking money or the necessities of life.

clue.text: Napier took it for pun

parts.note: General Napier, after conquering an Indian province, supposedly sent the one-word Latin message Peccavi, I have sinned

explanation.surface: A Victorian general seized something for the sake of a joke.
explanation.walkthrough: Napier took the province in 1843; the famous Peccavi telegram, 'I have sinned', puns on its name.
explanation.definitionFit: The province, now in Pakistan, conquered by Napier and punned on in his reputed telegram.

clue.text: Set out to trap King — he's landed in Scotland

indicators.note: to trap means the first word encloses the king's letter

parts.note: laid means set out, as a table
R, for rex, is the abbreviation for king

explanation.surface: A snare is laid for a king who has come ashore in Scotland.
explanation.walkthrough: 'landed' suggests coming ashore; here it means owning land.
explanation.definitionFit: A Scottish landowner of an estate.

clue.text: Like Gray's tenor or Keats' sweeter melodies?

definitions.text: Like Gray's tenor or Keats' sweeter melodies?

parts.words: Like Gray's tenor or Keats' sweeter melodies?
parts.note: Gray's Elegy speaks of the quiet tenor of humble lives, and Keats says unheard melodies are sweeter

explanation.surface: Comparing a singer in Gray's poem with Keats's sweeter tunes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tenor' suggests a singer but means the course of life in Gray's Elegy; Keats's Ode on a Grecian Urn: 'Heard melodies are sweet, but those unheard / Are sweeter'.
explanation.definitionFit: Silent, making no sound, as both poets' lines describe.

clue.text: Take steps to put in safe what's highly valued

indicators.note: to put in means the safe word goes inside the steps word

parts.note: to tread is to take steps
sure means safe, certain

explanation.surface: Precautions are taken to store valuables in a safe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'safe' looks like the strongbox but is the adjective SURE, placed inside TREAD by 'to put in'.
explanation.definitionFit: Cherished things are those held most dear.

clue.text: Office initially held by male a year

definitions.text: Office initially held by male a year

indicators.note: held by means the first letter sits inside the following pieces
initially means the first letter of the word

explanation.surface: A post traditionally held by a man for one year.
explanation.walkthrough: 'initially' takes O from 'Office' and 'held by' puts it inside M, A, YR. The whole clue also describes a civic post held for a year.
explanation.definitionFit: Town and city civic heads traditionally serve one-year terms.
